content:
I’d like to invite you to discuss the goals of the Lean Kernel Arena, and what we consider “fair play” on it. This is surfacing a discussion that started in DMs, with some disagreement of what’s good sportsmanship on the arena, and how much ambition is healthy. I’ll lay out my idea and vision for the arena, and am interesting to hear what you all have to say as well.

What is a good checker?

My motivation for the Lean Kernel Arena was to spur the development for more Lean checkers, and have a site that shows them all, with some metrics as I was able to come up with. I did intentionally call it an “arena” and not a “competition” though, because I don’t think there can be a good meaningful competition for Lean checkers.

So, what is a good checker? I would say, a good checker for Lean is

  1. consistent: does not accept false “proofs”
  2. complete: accepts all valid proofs (or at least those practically relevant)
  3. efficient: does that quickly and with little memory.

What are we measuring (spoiler: not a “goodness”)

It may seem like the arena is measuring that, but of course it is not. It measures “does this checker handle these particular fixed test cases” and “how many instructions does this checker use while doing that”. These are rather weak proxies for the real goals.

There are so many ways in which you can move up in the arena’s table’s sorting (let me avoid the term “ranking”) while still regressing on the lists above. Change the code t use fewer but slower instructions. Disable threading because instruction counting doesn’t reward the (very very practically) useful feature of parallelism. Change the checker to the one-liner “exit 0 if input is mathlib-sized, else decline”.

Therefore I think that whoever optimizes for the arena ranking primarily is missing the point, and is not doing something useful.

Intrinsic goals for writing checkers

Instead, I am hoping checker authors have their own goals, independent of the arena. That could be, among other things,

  • “write the best checker (see above)”. It could also be
  • “write the best checker given a certain design idea (e.g. nanoclo)”, or
  • “write the best checker than I can still verify (con-leche)”, or
  • “write the simplest checker, as a reference (mini)” or
  • “write a checker in TeX for the lullz (overfull)”.

As you advance toward your goal, then maybe (hopefully) the metrics on the arena improve. Then I hope you are happy about it.
But maybe they don’t (e.g. when you introduce parallelism). Then I hope you can be magnanimus about it.

Conversely, if you find yourself making a change that only makes sense because of the arena, and that looks odd on its own, then maybe recall your own goals?

Also, if you make a change that improves your ranking, but that is clearly something that could and should be done uniformly (ok, only “number of threads” come to my mind), then the thing to do in the spirit of collaboration is to bring this up here and discuss how and if we should handle that collectively.

That said, maybe your goal is to optimize for the arena’s metrics, whether they are practically useful or not, because optimizing for a hard, fixed, measurable metric is what you want to do. Then I will not stop you. If that’s the case, then maybe it’s best to clarify that in the checker’s description and README, that this checker is turned for an artificial metric, and not for some intrinsic goal.

PS: Why no competition

(It was suggested that instead of all this vague and moraly talk I should just fix the arena to measure more closely what I think that checkers should optimize for. I disagree; it is technically really hard, as you need much more resources to measure wall-time meaningfully, soundness and completeness are even harder to measure, and even then it wouldn’t be the right measure for every kernel out there, e.g. wouldn’t take “verified” or “parallel” into account. In the end, Goodhart’s law is hard to argue with.)

Here is my take (I am the author of sokonanoda). It's evident that every checker has vastly different goals, so my opinion would be that there really shouldn't be any sorted order; personally I would prefer if it were just alphabetised, and then you sort by whatever column you want after.
I am sort of uncompetitive; tbh as soon as it became clear that yes, "surprise, NbE is faster than substitution", there was not really much point comparing with other checkers in terms of raw speed. I am not worried about any sort of sorting order or ranking. Please fork my checker and make it faster!

FYI, I pointed Claude to Sokonanoda to try to optimize it, here is what it says so far:

┌─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
│       Export        │ Wall, upstream → modified │ CPU, upstream → modified │
├─────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ init                │ 4.6 → 3.2 s (−30 %)       │ 15.2 → 12.3 s (−19 %)    │
├─────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ std                 │ 7.8 → 5.3 s (−32 %)       │ 27.1 → 20.7 s (−24 %)    │
├─────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ cedar               │ 12.3 → 8.8 s (−28 %)      │ 43.2 → 34.7 s (−20 %)    │
├─────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ con-leche           │ 13.8 → 12.0 s (−13 %)     │ 50.5 → 46.0 s (−9 %)     │
├─────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ navier-stokes-euler │ 22.3 → 18.1 s (−19 %)     │ 79.1 → 72.2 s (−9 %)     │
├─────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ cslib               │ 30.6 → 20.1 s (−34 %)     │ 102.7 → 79.7 s (−22 %)   │
├─────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ mathlib             │ 87.7 → 59.6 s (−32 %)     │ 299.1 → 237.5 s (−21 %)  │
└─────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘

The two changes

  1. Shorter cache sessions. The evaluator's caches are now dropped after 2 MB of arena use instead of 16 MB, which
    keeps the tables cache-resident. This alone cut mathlib CPU time by about 17 % and has no soundness impact, since
    it only changes when caches are emptied.

  2. Checking while parsing. For inputs of 32 MB or more with more than one thread, the parser publishes immutable
    snapshots as it goes and the checker threads start on them immediately. Standard input that is a regular file is
    now memory-mapped rather than read.

I think I will let it play a bit more. But it is more of a question, what could we do with an optimized AI-written checker? Could we trust it? Or just see it as what could be possible in principle? Or trust it after we can get it through Aeneas?
By the way, it turns out that the checker relies on 128-bit hashes not colliding, so proving might be challenging. Edit: Claude says it could remove this hash-reliance without notable speed sacrifice.

I am wairy of tweaking perf by keeping caches small. Some caches are practically relevant for completeness: if you don't cache them then proof terms with sharing explode in size exponentially. So some caches (Bette called memo tables) are correctness-relevant. Only measuring mathlib and optimizing for that means it quickly falls over on other proofs. Again, different incentives whether you want to compete in the arena or build a reliable checker.

I indeed told it to optimize primarily against Mathlib. My initial thought was that it could exploit some typical patterns, which might, or might not generalize to other proofs. Didn't expect that tweaking cache size would be the first & most productive thing it would do :sweat_smile:. On the other hand, I thought Mathlib & Navies-Stokes are reasonably big projects, what are the proofs that would be harmed by this cache reduction?

My initial thinking was that I would let AI improve a checker as long as it can give guarantees that it is sound. But then I thought it might be a good experiment to see how far it can get without such strict rules (when it just takes soundness on its own judgement).

In con-ron I just ran into a case where a arbitrary cache size limit caused a real regression:

Claude analysis

Example: evicting a cache at an arbitrary size limit creates a performance cliff

Where: con-ron, a Rust port of the con-leche Lean kernel checker, on the lean-kernel-arena test perf/magma-list-deep-n36.

Symptom: on almost every input, con-ron executes about 45 % of con-leche's instructions. On this one test it executed 128 % of con-leche's and 169 % of nanoda's (391.7 G instructions against 305.4 G and 232 G). Its smaller sibling magma-list-deep-n21 was normal (0.47×).

Cause: the port added a safety limit that the original does not have. Its whnf_core memo table is dropped entirely once it reaches 4 194 304 entries (CACHE_CAP, annotated "con-leche: none"). One declaration in n36 (countermodel) needs about 14.5 M entries in that table, so the table filled up and was dropped 11 times in that one declaration. After each drop the checker redid the same β-reductions to rebuild the same entries (57 % of the profile under whnf_app → instantiate → intern_app).

Two details make this a poor trade:
- It saved no memory. The memo maps term handles to term handles, and the terms themselves are hash-consed and stay alive in the term store. Dropping the memo freed only the table, while recomputation re-interned nodes that already existed.
- It was invisible until a large input. Init and all of Mathlib never reach the limit, so every regular benchmark looked fine. The cost appears suddenly, as a cliff, once one declaration crosses the threshold. Below the limit the cost is 0; above it, it grows with (number of evictions) × (cost of rebuilding the table).

Fix: raise the limit to 2^25, where it is a bound on pathological memory rather than a working-set size. With that, n36 takes 147.1 G instructions, 0.48× con-leche, the usual ratio, and is identical to running with no limit at all. Init is unaffected. With the limit gone, con-ron and con-leche scale the same from n21 to n36 (×12.0 and ×11.7).

A second, related bug: resizing a table when it is cleared. Between declarations, con-ron clears its per-declaration tables and pre-sizes each new table from how full the old one was. That target is half load, but tables only grow at ¾ load. So a table that ended between ½ and ¾ full was reallocated at twice its size, while the old one was still alive. On n36 that is a 2^27-slot hash-cons table, a single 2.7 GB allocation, which aborted the run under an 8 GiB cap after the hard declaration had already been checked. Not pre-sizing tables of 2^20 slots or more brings n36's peak memory to 3.2 GB, at no cost on Init. (Never pre-sizing at all costs 0.46 %: small tables do benefit from it.)

Lessons:
- A memo that is dropped whole at a fixed size turns "slightly over the limit" into "repeatedly recompute everything". If memory must be bounded, the bound should sit far above any realistic working set, or eviction should be partial or by generation, never "clear all".
- Measure where the memory actually lives first. Here the memo is cheap and the term store is not, so the limit protected nothing.
- Benchmarks below the threshold cannot reveal a cliff. Adversarial or scaled inputs, like the arena's magma-* family, are what show it.
- A sizing heuristic for clearing (or rehashing) a table must agree with the table's growth rule, or "clear" becomes "grow".
But it sounded like the cache was already previously evicted at an arbitrary size limit?
Yes, it was previously so, but I think it was misguided.

Some findings to this: for Tenet I tried setting the .NET GC heap count on the arena run line. On the big corpora it looked free: peak memory went from 3.03 GB to 2.09 GB for the same instructions. But the single-declaration perf tests got 10 to 17% more expensive, so I pulled it.

On caches: Tenet keeps its reduction caches per declaration and never clears them mid-declaration, so the con-ron style cliff can't happen there.

I was using Lean Kernel Arena as a differential testing tool for soundness bugs, but then I realized maybe not a good idea since each of the kernels' implementations could be buggy. Maybe gently warn people that this might not be a ground truth people should take for granted? I'm curious on how others have used Lean Kernel Arena as an oracle for what, and if it did turn out to be useful.
